slides.text: A new chat system ships with working federation, IRC compatibility, full docs, even tests. Read closely and it's re-implementing **roughly half of XMPP**, a protocol that already solved the same problem years ago.
The project's commit history shows it was built fast with an AI coding assistant, working code and tests, end to end. **Nobody stopped to check what already existed.**

One developer in the discussion put it directly: this is **a poorly specified implementation of half of XMPP.** He'd seen the pattern before: people building deep into a domain without ever touching the existing work in that field.

Not everyone in the thread agreed reuse was the answer. Another developer replied that **XMPP itself is a genuinely painful protocol to implement.** Prior art isn't automatically worth reusing, even when it exists.

A sharper gap: one engineer asked how the project plans to stop bad actors spinning up unlimited servers and spamming at scale. **No answer showed up in the docs.** Federated systems spend years hardening against exactly that.

panel.small: answers to the spam question, in the docs

slides.text: Another developer asked the more basic question: why build a new federated network at all, instead of extending one that already exists, like Matrix or ActivityPub? **Every new protocol restarts the hardening clock at zero.**

Before you ship something an AI assistant scaffolded, especially anything touching identity, federation, or security: **spend an hour on prior art first.** Ask what already tried this, and why it held up or didn't.
When you review AI-written code, you check it for bugs. Start checking it for reinvention too: **is this solving a problem someone already solved,** with the failure modes already known?
Have you shipped, or caught, something AI-assisted that reinvented an existing standard, worse? **Tell me what broke first,** and save this for your next AI-assisted project.
